tweet_text:
if I interpret the spirit of your question as "is there a general method to compress higher dimensional feature spaces onto lower dimensional manifolds that preserves all the Important Features", the answer is no, but it might help to clarify a few things first:

we want to usefully compress information, because we operate on limited compute and can't see higher dimensional spaces in their totality. well, our best bet is to make a lossless compressor, guaranteeing we always keep the Important Things. sadly, we can't, we don't know how- (it's impossible: there's a simple argument re pigeonholing n binary strings into n-1 spaces, then source coding theorem, kolmogorov uncomputability, etc). 

short of that, we want an algorithm that keeps Most of the Important Patterns. but you can probably already see the problem here: we haven't defined what's important yet. we have some heuristics for this, but they vary across contexts. so we get trade-offs:
- PCA et al (Their Brutish Linear Methods) are fast but don't capture high d complexities like curvature,  disconnected surfaces, etc because they effectively flatten these. 
- Isomaps preserve global morphology, but have structural failure modes (breakdowns around holes, nonconvex sampling, etc)
- tsne/umap are great at capturing local structure but arbitrarily misrepresent global properties
- autoencoder flavours are the most 'generic' method because they enforce the least procedural complexity (most agnostic), but this trade-off also skews their learning rate so in low data regimes your mileage can be  worse than prescriptivist methods that Get Results because they bake in more specific patterns than "go figure out what to go figure out yourself". (note that a bunch of other methods actually just fall out as special subsets of AEs - eg PCA is just a linear autoencoder + mse, factor analysis is similar but with a guassian latent, etc)

all these algorithms form a construction by minimising some distortion measure, but doing this inevitably runs into Anscombe flavoured problems (maybe you've seen the memefied dinosaurus version of this) - you can only approximate facets of reconstruction fidelity and your chosen approximation will always be a lossy estimator

there's a lot of nuance not covered here, but essentially Different Methods ⇌ Different Strengths, Limitations Apply is the bitter state
